$$
{\lambda }_{1}=3\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=2.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we get 

$$
A-{\lambda }_{1}I=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

$$
A-{\lambda }_{2}I=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we get an eigenvector 
${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Now, we write down the general solution to the given linear system of differential equations: 

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]{e}^{2t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R\end{aligned}

:db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130393 :tutorial/content "We know how to solve a system of differential equations when they're decoupled. However, most systems are not decoupled. So, how do we solve them?

Let's consider a general linear system of two differential equations:

![](images/72/72a4d6a819a56d80818184e16205028a3a51eab2e97d1cdad72b8d495e5fd8d1.svg)

It turns out that if the matrix $A$ has two *distinct real eigenvalues* $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, then $A$ is diagonalizable and we can solve the system.

If the eigenvectors corresponding to $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ are ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2},$ respectively, then the general solution to our original system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.
$$

This result is true for any $n \times n$ system with $n$ distinct eigenvalues. We'll prove this result for a $2\times 2$ system at the end of the lesson.

Now, let's see some concrete examples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130359 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to solve a decoupled system of differential equations. Our goal now is to understand in more detail why this method works. 

Let's consider our general linear system of two differential equations once again:

![](images/65/6529692bc6317e2c675e756533a733c0caf087f3ac0b64b9c3a407924014d94b.svg)

We will show that if the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, we can convert it into an equivalent decoupled system.

If $A$ is diagonalizable, it has $2$ linearly independent eigenvectors ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}.$ We use these to form the *change of variables matrix* $E,$ given by

![](images/c1/c11833cbccd43c172ab7699a9000df5e2cf4bfedb0720958f1d5a407e5aeb8f2.svg)

Because the columns are linearly independent, $E$ is invertible. Then, the substitution  

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = E\mathbf{u}(t)
$$

will transform our original system of differential equations into a decoupled one, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(Eu(t)) & =A(Eu(t)) \\ E{u}^{′}(t) & =AEu(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={E}^{-1}AE\,u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that

![](images/c9/c9657a197b8232d883c6da546170754f2cc6916378d0c269755b3b5aae2173e0.svg)

is a diagonal matrix, and ${\color{red}\lambda_1},$ ${\color{blue}\lambda_2}$ are the eigenvalues of $A$ corresponding to ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}.$

Following these steps, we now have the *decoupled system*
![](images/55/557b8775c900635024b99ba9123d8023b2667db0459b1c8df53df886f4b156f8.svg)

Here, the matrix $D = E^{-1}$ is sometimes called the **decoupling matrix**.

Let's see a concrete example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130394 :tutorial/content "Consider the $2\times 2$ matrix differential equation

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t).
$$

 

Assume that $A$ is diagonalizable and has eigenvectors ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}$ with corresponding eigenvalues ${\color{red}\lambda_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\lambda_2},$ respectively.

We've been using the general solution formula 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}.
$$

But where does this formula come from? First, remember that the substitution

![](images/7e/7ece1267196b62dfffdf40b16af1b94e9169b6a798f7841f0fd361733042764f.svg)

transforms the matrix differential equation into the equivalent decoupled system

![](images/a6/a61af1176fb00e767ce5a8fc0ce349b79742937909f70c01701db56b126b010e.svg)

We can solve this new decoupled system using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the substitution $\mathbf{x}(t)=E\mathbf{u}(t)$, we can transform the system back to the variable $\mathbf x(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =Eu(t) \\  & =E({c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}E[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}E[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our original system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129398 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

If the eigenvectors corresponding to $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ are ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2},$ respectively, then the general solution to our original system can be written as

$$

$$

Now, let's see some concrete examples."] [17592186130359 :tutorial/content "We've seen how to solve a decoupled system of differential equations. Our goal now is to understand in more detail why this method works. 

Let's consider our general linear system of two differential equations once again:

![](images/65/6529692bc6317e2c675e756533a733c0caf087f3ac0b64b9c3a407924014d94b.svg)

We will show that if the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, we can convert it into an equivalent decoupled system.

If $A$ is diagonalizable, it has $2$ linearly independent eigenvectors ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}.$ We use these to form the *change of variables matrix* $E,$ given by

![](images/c1/c11833cbccd43c172ab7699a9000df5e2cf4bfedb0720958f1d5a407e5aeb8f2.svg)

Because the columns are linearly independent, $E$ is invertible. Then, the substitution  

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = E\mathbf{u}(t)
$$

will transform our original system of differential equations into a decoupled one, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(Eu(t)) & =A(Eu(t)) \\ E{u}^{′}(t) & =AEu(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={E}^{-1}AE\,u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that

![](images/c9/c9657a197b8232d883c6da546170754f2cc6916378d0c269755b3b5aae2173e0.svg)

is a diagonal matrix, and ${\color{red}\lambda_1},$ ${\color{blue}\lambda_2}$ are the eigenvalues of $A$ corresponding to ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}.$

Following these steps, we now have the *decoupled system*
![](images/55/557b8775c900635024b99ba9123d8023b2667db0459b1c8df53df886f4b156f8.svg)

Here, the matrix $D = E^{-1}$ is sometimes called the **decoupling matrix**.

$$

We've been using the general solution formula 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}.
$$

But where does this formula come from? First, remember that the substitution

![](images/7e/7ece1267196b62dfffdf40b16af1b94e9169b6a798f7841f0fd361733042764f.svg)

transforms the matrix differential equation into the equivalent decoupled system

![](images/a6/a61af1176fb00e767ce5a8fc0ce349b79742937909f70c01701db56b126b010e.svg)

We can solve this new decoupled system using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =Eu(t) \\  & =E({c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}) \\  & ={c}_{1}E[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}E[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}\end{aligned}
$$

:tutorial/content "We know how to solve a system of differential equations when they're decoupled. However, most systems are not decoupled. So, how do we solve them?

Let's consider a general linear system of two differential equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{'}(t)=a\,{x}_{1}(t)+b\,{x}_{2}(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{'}(t)=c\,{x}_{1}(t)+d\,{x}_{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

It turns out that if the matrix $A$ has two *distinct real eigenvalues* $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, then $A$ is diagonalizable and we can solve the system.

If the eigenvectors corresponding to $\color{red}\lambda_1$ and $\color{blue}\lambda_2$ are ${\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2},$ respectively, then the general solution to our original system can be written as

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = c_1{\color{red}\mathbf{v}_1} e^{{\color{red}\lambda_1} t} + c_2{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} e^{{\color{blue}\lambda_2} t}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.
